pos: n. (a sea-going vessel; rendering Hebrew oniyah, Greek ploion)
etymology: Saxon scip. In the Gospels the ship is Peter's workplace, Christ's pulpit, and the storm-tossed figure of the church; in Paul's letters it becomes a warning.
biblical_def: The ship in Scripture is a working boat before it is a symbol, and the symbolism grows out of the work. Jonah's flight begins with one: “he found a ship going to Tarshish: so he paid the fare thereof, and went down into it, to go with them unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD” (Jon 1:3) — a man can always find a ship going where he wants to go, and the fare is always payable, and it never reaches the destination he intends. In Galilee the same vessel becomes a pulpit: “he entered into one of the ships, which was Simon's… and he sat down, and taught the people out of the ship” (Luk 5:3), the Lord borrowing a fisherman's boat and paying for it with a catch. In the storm the ship carries the disciples' whole fear: “there arose a great storm of wind, and the waves beat into the ship, so that it was now full” (Mar 4:37). And Paul turns it into the sharpest warning about apostasy in the pastoral epistles — men “concerning faith have made shipwreck” (1Ti 1:19), having first put away a good conscience.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ship as a vessel of a particular kind of rigging, and in general any large vessel navigated on the ocean with sails.
webster_full: SHIP, n. In a general sense, a vessel or building of a peculiar structure, adapted to navigation.
2. In an appropriate sense, a building of a structure or form fitted for navigation, furnished with a bowsprit and three masts.
SHIPWRECK, n. The destruction of a ship by being cast ashore or broken to pieces by beating against rocks.
2. The parts of a shattered ship.
scriptures: Jon 1:3

But Jonah rose up to flee unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD, and went down to Joppa; and he found a ship going to Tarshish: so he paid the fare thereof, and went down into it, to go with them unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD.
Luk 5:3
And he entered into one of the ships, which was Simon's, and prayed him that he would thrust out a little from the land. And he sat down, and taught the people out of the ship.
Mar 4:37
And there arose a great storm of wind, and the waves beat into the ship, so that it was now full.
Holding faith, and a good conscience; which some having put away concerning faith have made shipwreck:
corruption_summary: Shipwreck of the faith is now spoken of as though it happened suddenly and without cause; Paul names the cause exactly — a good conscience put away first, and the faith lost afterward.
corruption_paragraphs: Public accounts of leaving the faith are usually framed as intellectual: questions that could not be answered, arguments that failed, a slow honest reckoning. Paul's order in 1 Timothy 1:19 is different and is worth stating plainly. Holding faith and a good conscience is the paired charge; the shipwreck comes to those who, having put away the good conscience, then make shipwreck concerning faith. Conscience goes first. The arguments are recruited afterward to justify a course already steered, which is why apologetics alone so rarely recovers a man who has been living against his conscience for years.

Jonah's ship makes the same point from the other end. The fare was payable, the vessel was sailing, and every circumstance cooperated with his rebellion — providence is not obliged to block the road to Tarshish. The storm that followed was not an obstacle to God's purpose but the instrument of it, and the sailors who threw him overboard ended up fearing the LORD exceedingly and offering a sacrifice. A conscience put away can still buy a ticket; it cannot outrun the sea.
roots_summary: Hebrew oniyah (H591), a ship; Greek ploion (G4143), a boat or vessel — the fisherman's trade, the Lord's pulpit, and Paul's figure for apostasy.
roots_lines: Hebrew oniyah (H591) — a ship; Jonah's ship to Tarshish (Jon 1:3) and the ships of Tarshish in the prophets.
Greek ploion (G4143) — a boat, ship; Simon's ship used as a pulpit (Luk 5:3) and the ship filling with water (Mar 4:37).
Greek nauageō (G3489) — to suffer shipwreck; used literally by Paul of himself (2Co 11:25) and figuratively of the faith (1Ti 1:19).
usage: “He found a ship going to Tarshish: so he paid the fare thereof” — rebellion is rarely obstructed early.
“He sat down, and taught the people out of the ship” — a borrowed boat, repaid with a catch.
“Concerning faith have made shipwreck” — and the conscience was put away first.

pos: n. (a mesh for taking fish or game; hence a snare; rendering Hebrew resheth, Greek diktuon)
etymology: Saxon net, from knittan, to knit. Scripture uses it in two opposite directions — the net Christ fills, and the net the enemy sets.
biblical_def: A net in Scripture is either an instrument of gathering or an instrument of entrapment, and the difference is whose hand holds it. Christ fills nets. To a fisherman at the end of a fruitless night He gives a word to obey against experience: “Master, we have toiled all the night, and have taken nothing: nevertheless at thy word I will let down the net” (Luk 5:5) — the whole of Christian obedience is in that nevertheless. After the resurrection the catch is counted and the mesh holds: “Simon Peter went up, and drew the net to land full of great fishes, an hundred and fifty and three: and for all there were so many, yet was not the net broken” (Joh 21:11). The kingdom itself is a net: “the kingdom of heaven is like unto a net, that was cast into the sea, and gathered of every kind” (Mat 13:47) — a visible church of every kind, sorted at the shore and not before. But there is also a net set for the feet, and the psalmist knows who cuts it: “Mine eyes are ever toward the LORD; for he shall pluck my feet out of the net” (Psa 25:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines net as an instrument for catching fish and fowls, made with twine or thread interwoven with meshes; and figuratively a snare or device to entrap.
webster_full: NET, n. An instrument for catching fish and fowls, or wild beasts, formed with twine or thread interwoven with meshes.
2. A cunning device; a snare.
NET, v.t. To make a net or net-work.
NETTING, n. A piece of net-work.
scriptures: Luk 5:5
And Simon answering said unto him, Master, we have toiled all the night, and have taken nothing: nevertheless at thy word I will let down the net.
Simon Peter went up, and drew the net to land full of great fishes, an hundred and fifty and three: and for all there were so many, yet was not the net broken.
Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto a net, that was cast into the sea, and gathered of every kind:
Mine eyes are ever toward the LORD; for he shall pluck my feet out of the net.
corruption_summary: The parable of the net has been replaced by an assumption of a pure visible church, so that every discovery of an unconverted member is treated as a scandal rather than as the thing Christ said to expect until the shore.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 13:47 says the net gathers of every kind and that the sorting happens when it is drawn to shore — at the end of the world, by angels, not by the congregation in the meantime. Two errors ignore this. The first is a purism that treats the discovery of hypocrisy as proof that the church has failed, and reacts by ever finer screening at the door. The second is the opposite complacency, which concludes that since the net holds every kind, no sorting matters and discipline is uncharitable. Christ's parable authorises neither: the church exercises real discipline for real, known sin, while expecting that the final separation is not hers to make.

Luke 5 gives the working posture. Peter had professional grounds for refusing — wrong hour, wrong water, and a night's evidence — and he let the net down anyway on the bare word of Christ. The catch that followed did not make him confident; it made him fall down and confess himself a sinful man. Nets filled at Christ's word do not produce swagger in those who haul them.
roots_summary: Hebrew resheth (H7568), a net or snare; Greek diktuon (G1350), a fishing net, and sagēnē (G4522), a dragnet — the gathering of the kingdom and the snare of the enemy.
roots_lines: Hebrew resheth (H7568) — a net, snare; “he shall pluck my feet out of the net” (Psa 25:15).
Greek diktuon (G1350) — a fishing net; the unbroken net of Joh 21:11.
Greek sagēnē (G4522) — a large dragnet swept through the sea; the kingdom parable of Mat 13:47.
usage: “Nevertheless at thy word I will let down the net” — obedience against experience.
“Yet was not the net broken” — a hundred and fifty and three, and the mesh held.
“The kingdom of heaven is like unto a net… gathered of every kind” — sorted at the shore.

pos: n. (the atmosphere; the region between earth and heaven; rendering Hebrew shamayim, Greek aēr)
etymology: From Greek aēr through Latin. In Scripture the air is a real domain with a real ruler — and the place appointed for the meeting of the Lord with His own.
biblical_def: The air in Scripture is the lower heaven, the region between the ground and the sky, and it is not empty. Paul assigns it a ruler: believers once walked “according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that now worketh in the children of disobedience” (Eph 2:2) — a real dominion, presently exercised, over men in unbelief. It is also the homeliest of images for the ordinary creation: “the birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head” (Mat 8:20), the Maker of the birds with less provision than they. Paul uses it for wasted effort in the Christian race: “so fight I, not as one that beateth the air” (1Co 9:26) — a boxer swinging at nothing, which is what undisciplined religion amounts to. And Thessalonians puts the last word in the same domain: “we which are alive and remain shall be caught up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air: and so shall we ever be with the Lord” (1Th 4:17). The territory the prince of the power of the air presently claims is the very place his conqueror will be met.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines air as the fluid which we breathe, surrounding the earth; also the open space above, and figuratively mien or manner.
webster_full: AIR, n. The fluid which we breathe. Air is inodorous, invisible, insipid, colorless, elastic, possessed of gravity, easily moved, rarefied, and condensed.
2. Air, in motion; a light breeze.
3. Vent; utterance abroad; publication; publicity.
4. A tune; a short song or piece of music.
5. The peculiar look, appearance, manner or mien of a person.
scriptures: Eph 2:2
Wherein in time past ye walked according to the course of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that now worketh in the children of disobedience:
Mat 8:20
And Jesus saith unto him, The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head.
I therefore so run, not as uncertainly; so fight I, not as one that beateth the air:
Then we which are alive and remain shall be caught up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air: and so shall we ever be with the Lord.
corruption_summary: The prince of the power of the air is treated either as first-century superstition or as a figure to be conjured at in warfare rituals — where Paul names him soberly as the spirit now working in the children of disobedience.
corruption_paragraphs: Liberal readings dissolve Ephesians 2:2 into ancient cosmology, leaving unbelief as sociology and habit with no personal enemy behind it. Certain charismatic teachings go the other way, mapping the air into territorial hierarchies to be bound by name in prayer marches and warfare formulas. Paul does neither. He names the prince once, in a sentence whose main point is what we were — dead in trespasses, walking according to the course of this world — and whose next word is But God, who is rich in mercy. The devil appears in the passage as part of the account of our helplessness, not as the object of a technique.

This is why the cure Paul prescribes is not incantation but armour, truth, and prayer, and why 1 Corinthians 9 matters here. A Christian beating the air is expending real energy on nothing — activity mistaken for warfare. The apostle's alternative is unglamorous: he keeps under his body and brings it into subjection. Meanwhile the promise of 1 Thessalonians 4 settles the question of who owns the sky, and it is not the prince presently in it.
roots_summary: Hebrew shamayim (H8064), the heavens, including the lower air; Greek aēr (G109), the atmosphere — a real domain with a usurping prince and an appointed meeting.
roots_lines: Hebrew shamayim (H8064) — heaven, sky; the fowl of the heaven, rendered “birds of the air” throughout the Authorized Version.
Greek aēr (G109) — the air, the lower atmosphere; the prince of its power (Eph 2:2) and the meeting place of 1Th 4:17.
Greek ouranos (G3772) — heaven; distinguished in usage from aēr, the region nearer the earth.
usage: “The prince of the power of the air” — a real dominion over men in unbelief.
“The birds of the air have nests” — the Maker with less provision than His creatures.
“To meet the Lord in the air” — the usurper's territory chosen for the meeting.

pos: n. (a swell or billow of water; rendering Hebrew gal, mishbar, Greek kuma, kludōn)
etymology: Saxon wafian, to fluctuate. Scripture's waves are the standing figure for instability — in the sea, in the doubter, and in the false teacher.
biblical_def: A wave in Scripture is motion without direction, and it becomes the Bible's picture of three things. Of affliction: “Deep calleth unto deep at the noise of thy waterspouts: all thy waves and thy billows are gone over me” (Psa 42:7) — and note the possessive, thy waves; the psalmist assigns his floods to God rather than to chance, which is the only reason he can go on to hope in Him. Of danger: “there arose a great storm of wind, and the waves beat into the ship, so that it was now full” (Mar 4:37). Of the divided mind: “let him ask in faith, nothing wavering. For he that wavereth is like a wave of the sea driven with the wind and tossed” (Jas 1:6) — a man who prays while reserving judgment is not asking, he is drifting. And of the false teacher, in Jude's brutal image: “Raging waves of the sea, foaming out their own shame” (Jud 1:13). The sea is loud, impressive, restless, and it produces nothing but foam. So does a ministry without truth.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines wave as a moving swell or volume of water, a billow; and to waver as to fluctuate, to be unsettled in opinion.
webster_full: WAVE, n. A moving swell or volume of water; usually, a swell raised and driven by wind.
2. Unevenness; inequality of surface.
3. The line or streak of luster on cloth watered and calendered.
WAVER, v.i. To play or move to and fro; to fluctuate; to be unsettled in opinion.
scriptures: Psa 42:7
Deep calleth unto deep at the noise of thy waterspouts: all thy waves and thy billows are gone over me.
Mar 4:37
And there arose a great storm of wind, and the waves beat into the ship, so that it was now full.
Jas 1:6
But let him ask in faith, nothing wavering. For he that wavereth is like a wave of the sea driven with the wind and tossed.
Jud 1:13
Raging waves of the sea, foaming out their own shame; wandering stars, to whom is reserved the blackness of darkness for ever.
corruption_summary: Doubt has been promoted from an ailment to a virtue — the honest posture of a thoughtful faith — where James calls the wavering man unstable in all his ways and tells him not to expect an answer.
corruption_paragraphs: A large body of contemporary religious writing treats settled conviction as arrogance and perpetual questioning as maturity, so that the man James describes as a wave driven and tossed is recast as the model believer. James is blunt in the other direction: let him not think that he shall receive any thing of the Lord. This is not a rebuke of the man who brings real perplexity to God — the psalms are full of that, and Psalm 42 is one of them. It is a rebuke of asking while withholding trust, praying with one hand and hedging with the other.

The distinction is visible in Psalm 42 itself. The psalmist is overwhelmed, and he says so; but he calls the billows thine, and he preaches to his own soul to hope in God. That is faith under water, not wavering. Jude then shows where cultivated instability ends when it takes up a pulpit: raging waves foaming out their own shame — noise, motion, and nothing left on the sand.
roots_summary: Hebrew gal (H1530), a heap or wave, and mishbar (H4867), a breaker; Greek kuma (G2949), a wave, and kludōn (G2830), a surge — instability in the sea and in the soul.
roots_lines: Hebrew gal (H1530) — a wave, billow, heap; “all thy waves and thy billows are gone over me” (Psa 42:7).
Greek kuma (G2949) — a wave, billow; the waves beating into the ship (Mar 4:37) and the raging waves of Jud 1:13.
Greek kludōn (G2830) — a surge or tossing; the wave of the sea driven with the wind (Jas 1:6).
usage: “All thy waves and thy billows are gone over me” — the floods assigned to God, not to chance.
“He that wavereth is like a wave of the sea” — motion mistaken for honesty.
“Raging waves of the sea, foaming out their own shame” — the false teacher, described.

pos: n. (the sensation or condition of warmth; the burden of the day; rendering Hebrew chom, Greek kauma)
etymology: Saxon hætu, from hat, hot. Scripture uses heat for the ordinary weight of labour and for the affliction from which God Himself is the shade.
biblical_def: Heat in Scripture is the daily burden of a working world and, in prophecy, the affliction God shields His people from. The covenant with Noah fixes it in the order of creation: “While the earth remaineth, seedtime and harvest, and cold and heat, and summer and winter, and day and night shall not cease” (Gen 8:22) — heat is not an intruder but a promise, part of the rhythm God swore to maintain. It is the measure of honest labour, and of grumbling: the first-hired complain that the latecomers “have wrought but one hour, and thou hast made them equal unto us, which have borne the burden and heat of the day” (Mat 20:12). Isaiah promises a shelter: “there shall be a tabernacle for a shadow in the daytime from the heat, and for a place of refuge, and for a covert from storm and from rain” (Isa 4:6). And Revelation ends it: “They shall hunger no more, neither thirst any more; neither shall the sun light on them, nor any heat” (Rev 7:16). Heat is the world's ordinary cost, God's appointed shade, and one of the things heaven abolishes.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines heat as the sensation produced by the approach of fire; the cause of that sensation; hot weather; and figuratively ardor, vehemence, or violent passion.
webster_full: HEAT, n. Heat, as a cause of sensation, that is, the matter of heat, is considered to be a subtil fluid.
2. Hot air; hot weather; as the heat of the tropical climates.
3. Any accumulation or concentration of the matter of heat.
4. The state of being once hot or heated.
5. Animation in thought or discourse; vehemence; ardor; fervency.
scriptures: Gen 8:22
While the earth remaineth, seedtime and harvest, and cold and heat, and summer and winter, and day and night shall not cease.
Saying, These last have wrought but one hour, and thou hast made them equal unto us, which have borne the burden and heat of the day.
Isa 4:6
And there shall be a tabernacle for a shadow in the daytime from the heat, and for a place of refuge, and for a covert from storm and from rain.
Rev 7:16
They shall hunger no more, neither thirst any more; neither shall the sun light on them, nor any heat.
corruption_summary: The burden and heat of the day is now advanced as a claim on God — long service treated as earning a larger wage — which is precisely the grievance the parable was told to answer.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 20 is one of the hardest parables for religious people because the complaint is so reasonable. The men who bore the heat did more work; they were paid what they agreed; and they resent the equality. The householder's answer refuses their premise entirely: is thine eye evil, because I am good? Grace is not a wage scale, and long service in the vineyard confers no claim beyond the covenant already struck. Wherever a church begins to reckon seniority as merit — older members owed more voice, more deference, more consideration than newcomers converted last year — the murmuring of the first-hired has begun.

Genesis 8 and Revelation 7 frame the parable's heat honestly. It is real; God appointed it; it will not cease while the earth remains; and it is not for ever. The believer labours in genuine sun, is given a genuine covert in the meantime, and is promised a day when no heat shall light on him at all. That is the answer to grievance — not that the work was light, but that the wage was always grace and the shade was always God's.
roots_summary: Hebrew chom (H2527), heat, warmth; Greek kauma (G2738), burning heat, and kausōn (G2742), the scorching wind — the day's burden and heaven's abolition of it.
roots_lines: Hebrew chom (H2527) — heat; “cold and heat, and summer and winter” in the Noahic covenant (Gen 8:22).
Greek kausōn (G2742) — burning heat, the scorching east wind; “the burden and heat of the day” (Mat 20:12).
Greek kauma (G2738) — heat, scorching; “nor any heat” in the promise of Rev 7:16.
usage: “Cold and heat, and summer and winter… shall not cease” — heat sworn into the created order.
“Which have borne the burden and heat of the day” — long service mistaken for a claim.
“Neither shall the sun light on them, nor any heat” — the day's burden finally lifted.

pos: n. pl. (circular frames turning on an axle; rendering Hebrew ophan, galgal)
etymology: Saxon hweol. In Ezekiel the wheels are the vehicle of the glory; in Ecclesiastes a broken wheel is the end of a life.
biblical_def: Wheels in Scripture belong to chariots, to cisterns, and above all to Ezekiel's vision of the throne. There the prophet sees them beside the living creatures: “The appearance of the wheels and their work was like unto the colour of a beryl: and they four had one likeness: and their appearance and their work was as it were a wheel in the middle of a wheel” (Eze 1:16) — a construction that can move in any direction without turning, because the God whose throne it carries never has to change course. And the wheels do not move independently: “when the living creatures went, the wheels went by them: and when the living creatures were lifted up from the earth, the wheels were lifted up” (Eze 1:19). Nahum uses wheels for the terror of an army bearing down: “the noise of the rattling of the wheels, and of the pransing horses, and of the jumping chariots” (Nah 3:2). And Ecclesiastes uses one for the quiet end of a man: “or ever the silver cord be loosed… or the wheel broken at the cistern” (Ecc 12:6) — the mechanism that drew up water each morning, one day broken and not repaired.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines wheel as a circular frame turning on an axis, and notes its use for the machine that draws water and for the revolutions of fortune or life.
webster_full: WHEEL, n. A circular frame of wood, iron or other metal, consisting of a nave or hub, into which are inserted spokes.
2. A circular body.
3. A machine for spinning thread.
4. An instrument for torturing criminals.
5. A turn; a revolution; rotation.
scriptures: Eze 1:16
The appearance of the wheels and their work was like unto the colour of a beryl: and they four had one likeness: and their appearance and their work was as it were a wheel in the middle of a wheel.
Eze 1:19
And when the living creatures went, the wheels went by them: and when the living creatures were lifted up from the earth, the wheels were lifted up.
Nah 3:2
The noise of a whip, and the noise of the rattling of the wheels, and of the pransing horses, and of the jumping chariots.
Ecc 12:6
Or ever the silver cord be loosed, or the golden bowl be broken, or the pitcher be broken at the fountain, or the wheel broken at the cistern.
corruption_summary: Ezekiel's wheels have been handed over to speculation about ancient craft and machinery, which quietly changes the subject from the One seated above them to the vehicle beneath.
corruption_paragraphs: The wheels have attracted a century of speculation treating the vision as a report of visiting machinery. Whatever the appeal of that reading, it inverts the passage: Ezekiel describes the wheels in seventeen verses and then says that above the firmament was the likeness of a throne, and upon it the likeness as the appearance of a man — and falls on his face. The vision is a throne-chariot, and its point is that the glory of the LORD is mobile, going wherever the Spirit goes, and about to depart from a temple that presumed on His permanence.

That is the doctrine worth recovering. Judah believed the glory was fixed at Jerusalem by right, and Ezekiel watched it get up and leave on wheels. A congregation may likewise assume the presence of God is a fixture of its building and its history. The wheels say otherwise: they go where the Spirit goes, they are lifted when the living creatures are lifted, and nothing about the structure detains them. Ecclesiastes adds the personal version — one day the wheel at the cistern breaks, and the dust returns to the earth as it was.
roots_summary: Hebrew ophan (H212), a wheel, and galgal (H1534), a wheel or whirling thing — the throne-chariot of the glory, and the mechanism that finally breaks.
roots_lines: Hebrew ophan (H212) — a wheel; the wheels beside the living creatures (Eze 1:16, 19).
Hebrew galgal (H1534) — a wheel, whirlwind, rolling thing; the wheels of Eze 10:13, called O wheel.
The rabbinic name ophanim for an order of angels derives from this word, though Scripture itself calls them wheels, not creatures.
usage: “A wheel in the middle of a wheel” — movement in any direction without turning.
“When the living creatures were lifted up, the wheels were lifted up” — the glory is not fixed to a place.
“Or the wheel broken at the cistern” — the machinery of a life, one day not repaired.

pos: v.t. (to cover the surface of a thing with a layer of metal; rendering Hebrew tsaphah)
etymology: From over and lay. The tabernacle's furniture was acacia wood overlaid with gold — a construction Scripture describes in exhaustive detail and never apologises for.
biblical_def: To overlay is to case a thing in beaten metal, and it is the standard construction of the sanctuary: shittim wood within, pure gold without. Of the ark: “thou shalt overlay it with pure gold, within and without shalt thou overlay it, and shalt make upon it a crown of gold round about” (Exo 25:11) — gold on the inside too, where no eye would ever see it, because the workmanship was for God before it was for the congregation. Bezaleel executed it exactly: “he overlaid it with pure gold within and without, and made a crown of gold to it round about” (Exo 37:2). The boards and bars of the frame were treated the same way (Exo 26:29), and so was the altar of incense with its horns (Exo 30:3). The pattern is uniform: ordinary desert wood, given a covering it could not produce, made fit for the presence of God. Every believer stands on that principle. What is underneath is common; what is seen is a righteousness laid over it from outside, and the covering goes all the way in.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines overlay as to spread over, to cover on the surface, and to overwhelm or smother by lying upon.
webster_full: OVERLAY, v.t. To lay too much upon; to oppress with incumbent weight.
2. To cover on the surface; as, to overlay a table with a cloth.
3. To smother with too much or too close covering.
4. To spread over; as, to overlay with gold.
scriptures: And thou shalt overlay it with pure gold, within and without shalt thou overlay it, and shalt make upon it a crown of gold round about.
Exo 37:2
And he overlaid it with pure gold within and without, and made a crown of gold to it round about.
And thou shalt overlay the boards with gold, and make their rings of gold for places for the bars: and thou shalt overlay the bars with gold.
Exo 30:3
And thou shalt overlay it with pure gold, the top thereof, and the sides thereof round about, and the horns thereof; and thou shalt make unto it a crown of gold round about.
corruption_summary: Overlaid gold is dismissed as veneer — a show over cheap material — when Scripture makes the covering a picture of imputed righteousness and specifies gold on the hidden inner surface as well.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern instinct calls anything overlaid a fake: the real material is the wood, and the gold is presentation. Exodus 25 forbids that reading with one clause — within and without shalt thou overlay it. The inner surface, permanently hidden by the mercy seat and the tables of testimony, was gold too. The covering was not for the eye of the worshipper but for the character of the object, which is exactly the doctrine of imputation: the righteousness Christ lays over a believer is not a public varnish over a private ruin, it reaches where no congregation ever looks.

There is a real corruption to name, and it is the opposite one. Where a man supplies his own gold — reputation, respectability, doctrinal precision worn as plating over an unrenewed heart — the result is what our Lord called a whited sepulchre. The difference between the ark and the sepulchre is not whether there is a covering, but who applied it and how far in it goes. Bezaleel worked to a pattern given him; the Pharisees worked to one they chose.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsaphah (H6823), to overlay or plate with metal — the standard verb of tabernacle construction, wood cased in gold within and without.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsaphah (H6823) — to lay over, overlay, plate; used of the ark, the boards, the bars, the altar of incense and the table.
The base material is shittim wood (H7848), acacia — hard, desert-grown, and utterly common.
The same verb describes Solomon overlaying the house within with pure gold (1Ki 6:21) — the pattern carried from tent to temple.
usage: “Within and without shalt thou overlay it” — gold where no eye would ever see it.
“He overlaid it with pure gold” — Bezaleel working to a pattern he did not design.
“Thou shalt overlay the boards with gold” — common wood made fit for the presence.

pos: v.i. & v.t. (to move as air; to sound a trumpet; rendering Hebrew nashab, taqa, Greek pneō)
etymology: Saxon blawan, to breathe or blow. Scripture joins the two senses deliberately: the wind that blows where it will, and the trumpet a man is commanded to blow.
biblical_def: To blow covers two things in Scripture, and both are theological. First, the wind, which is sovereign and untraceable: “The wind bloweth where it listeth, and thou hearest the sound thereof, but canst not tell whence it cometh, and whither it goeth: so is every one that is born of the Spirit” (Joh 3:8). Our Lord uses the weather to teach Nicodemus that the new birth is observable in its effects and unmanageable in its cause. Isaiah applies the same wind to human pride: “The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: because the spirit of the LORD bloweth upon it: surely the people is grass” (Isa 40:7) — nations wither at a breath. Second, the trumpet, which is commanded and is a man's duty: “Blow ye the trumpet in Zion, and sound an alarm in my holy mountain: let all the inhabitants of the land tremble: for the day of the LORD cometh” (Joe 2:1), and in ordinary worship, “in your solemn days… ye shall blow with the trumpets over your burnt offerings” (Num 10:10). The wind is God's to send; the trumpet is ours to blow, and the watchman who does not blow it answers for the blood.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines blow as to make a current of air, to breathe, to sound a wind instrument, and to drive or impel by a current of air.
webster_full: BLOW, v.i. To make a current of air; to move as air.
2. To pant; to puff; to breathe hard or quick.
3. To breathe; as, to blow in a person's face.
4. To sound with being blown; as, the trumpet blows.
BLOW, v.t. To throw or drive a current of air upon; as, to blow the fire.
scriptures: Joh 3:8
The wind bloweth where it listeth, and thou hearest the sound thereof, but canst not tell whence it cometh, and whither it goeth: so is every one that is born of the Spirit.
Isa 40:7
The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: because the spirit of the LORD bloweth upon it: surely the people is grass.
Joe 2:1
Blow ye the trumpet in Zion, and sound an alarm in my holy mountain: let all the inhabitants of the land tremble: for the day of the LORD cometh, for it is nigh at hand;

Also in the day of your gladness, and in your solemn days, and in the beginnings of your months, ye shall blow with the trumpets over your burnt offerings, and over the sacrifices of your peace offerings; that they may be to you for a memorial before your God: I am the LORD your God.
corruption_summary: The Spirit's sovereignty in the new birth is regularly reversed — the wind made to blow where the church schedules it — while the trumpet a watchman is actually commanded to blow goes unsounded.
corruption_paragraphs: John 3:8 is one of the plainest statements of monergism in Scripture and one of the most inverted in practice. The wind blows where it listeth: the new birth is the Spirit's act, at His timing, by His choice, and no method controls it. Yet a great deal of modern religion is engineering designed to produce the wind on demand — the correct appeal, the correct atmosphere, the correct number of verses of the closing hymn — and the results are counted as births. Where the wind is manufactured, the church fills with people who were moved but never born.

The other failure is the neglected trumpet, and it is the opposite of passivity. Joel's command is unconditional: blow the trumpet in Zion, sound an alarm, the day of the LORD cometh. Ezekiel makes the watchman who sees the sword and does not blow personally liable for the blood. Sovereign wind and commanded trumpet stand together without strain in the same Bible: we cannot make a man live, and we are not excused from warning him.
roots_summary: Hebrew nashab (H5380), to blow as the wind, and taqa (H8628), to blow or blast a trumpet; Greek pneō (G4154), to blow or breathe — sovereign wind and commanded alarm.
roots_lines: Hebrew nashab (H5380) — to blow; “the spirit of the LORD bloweth upon it” (Isa 40:7).
Hebrew taqa (H8628) — to strike, clap, blast a trumpet; the command of Joe 2:1 and the trumpets of Num 10:10.
Greek pneō (G4154) — to blow, breathe; the wind of Joh 3:8, cognate with pneuma, spirit — the wordplay is the Lord's own.
usage: “The wind bloweth where it listeth” — the new birth is observable, not manageable.
“The spirit of the LORD bloweth upon it: surely the people is grass” — nations withered at a breath.
“Blow ye the trumpet in Zion” — the duty that is ours, and not optional.

pos: v.i. (to emit or reflect light; rendering Hebrew or, zarach, Greek lampō)
etymology: Saxon scinan, to shine. In Scripture God shines and men reflect — the order is never reversed.
biblical_def: To shine in Scripture is first something God does and only then something His people do. The priestly blessing asks for it as the highest good: “The LORD make his face shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee” (Num 6:25) — not that God would give things, but that He would turn His face and let it be bright toward the one blessed. Paul makes creation's first day the pattern of conversion: “God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, hath shined in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2Co 4:6) — the same fiat, the same absolute initiative, now in a human heart. From that, and only from that, comes the derived shining: “Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven” (Mat 5:16). Note where the glory lands — on the Father, not the lamp. And Daniel gives the end of it: “they that be wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament; and they that turn many to righteousness as the stars for ever and ever” (Dan 12:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines shine as to emit rays of light, to be bright, to be lively and animated, and to be conspicuous or eminent.
webster_full: SHINE, v.i. To emit rays of light; to give light; to beam with steady radiance; to exhibit brightness or splendor.
2. To be bright; to be lively and animated; as, to make the eyes shine.
3. To be gay or splendid.
4. To be beautiful.
5. To be eminent, conspicuous or distinguished.
scriptures: Num 6:25
The LORD make his face shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee:
For God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, hath shined in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.
Mat 5:16
Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven.
Dan 12:3
And they that be wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament; and they that turn many to righteousness as the stars for ever and ever.
corruption_summary: “Let your light shine” has become a slogan for self-expression and personal brilliance, though the verse itself sends every watching eye past the light to the Father.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 5:16 is quoted constantly as encouragement to be visible, gifted, unashamed of one's talents — and the second half of the sentence is dropped. Christ gives the purpose clause: that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven. A shining that terminates on the shiner has failed the verse regardless of how bright it is. The test is not whether people notice, but whom they praise afterward, and that test is uncomfortable in an age where personal brand is the currency of ministry as much as of commerce.

2 Corinthians 4 supplies the ground that makes the humility possible. The believer has nothing self-luminous about him; he is a clay vessel holding a light that was commanded into him by the same God who said Let there be light. Paul draws the conclusion in the next verse: the excellency of the power is of God, and not of us. Moses came down with a shining face and did not know it, which is the only safe condition in which to shine at all.
roots_summary: Hebrew or (H215), to be or become light, and zarach (H2224), to rise or shine forth; Greek lampō (G2989), to shine — God's face, the believer's lamp, and the wise as stars.
roots_lines: Hebrew or (H215) — to be light, to shine, to give light; “make his face shine upon thee” (Num 6:25).
Hebrew zarach (H2224) — to rise, break forth, shine; used of the sun rising and of light rising on the upright.
Greek lampō (G2989) — to shine, give light; the light shining before men (Mat 5:16) and shining in our hearts (2Co 4:6).
usage: “The LORD make his face shine upon thee” — the highest good asked for in the blessing.
“Hath shined in our hearts” — conversion described as the first day of creation repeated.
“That they may see your good works, and glorify your Father” — the clause that is always dropped.

pos: v.t. (to scatter in small drops; rendering Hebrew zaraq, nazah, Greek rhantizō)
etymology: From the Saxon; to scatter in drops. Sprinkling is the priestly application of blood — the moment at which a sacrifice already slain is applied to a particular person or thing.
biblical_def: To sprinkle is to apply blood or water in drops, and in Scripture it is the act by which a sacrifice already offered is brought into contact with the one it is for. On the Day of Atonement the high priest “shall take of the blood of the bullock, and sprinkle it with his finger upon the mercy seat eastward; and before the mercy seat shall he sprinkle of the blood with his finger seven times” (Lev 16:14) — the death has happened outside; the sprinkling puts it where God has said He will meet with His people. Isaiah promises the same action extended to the world: “So shall he sprinkle many nations; the kings shall shut their mouths at him” (Isa 52:15). Hebrews then names what the ceremony pointed to twice over: “let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience, and our bodies washed with pure water” (Heb 10:22), and, of the new covenant, “the blood of sprinkling, that speaketh better things than that of Abel” (Heb 12:24). Abel's blood cried for justice from the ground. This blood speaks better things, and it is sprinkled on the conscience.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sprinkle as to scatter in small drops or particles, to besprinkle, and to wash or cleanse by scattering water or blood upon.
webster_full: SPRINKLE, v.t. To scatter; to disperse; as water, a liquid, dust, powder, seed.
2. To scatter on; to disperse something over.
3. To wash; to cleanse; to purify.
SPRINKLING, n. The act of scattering in small drops or particles.
scriptures: And he shall take of the blood of the bullock, and sprinkle it with his finger upon the mercy seat eastward; and before the mercy seat shall he sprinkle of the blood with his finger seven times.
So shall he sprinkle many nations; the kings shall shut their mouths at him: for that which had not been told them shall they see; and that which they had not heard shall they consider.
Let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience, and our bodies washed with pure water.
And to Jesus the mediator of the new covenant, and to the blood of sprinkling, that speaketh better things than that of Abel.
corruption_summary: The sprinkled blood is treated as archaic ritual to be summarised past, yet Hebrews makes it the ground of a believer's access — and the sprinkling is on the conscience, not merely on the furniture.
corruption_paragraphs: Preaching that hurries past Leviticus loses the very category Hebrews needs. Without sprinkling, the death of Christ can be admired as an event and never applied as a transaction; the sinner is left believing in an atonement in general, with no answer to the question whether it is for him. Leviticus 16 supplies the answer's shape: blood shed at the altar, carried in, and put by a finger on the mercy seat — a specific application at a specific place for a specific people. Hebrews 10 relocates the finger to the conscience.

That relocation is the reason the epistle's conclusion is boldness rather than fear. An evil conscience is not managed by resolutions, forgotten by activity, or argued away; it is sprinkled. And Hebrews 12 gives the comparison that settles the matter: Abel's blood cried from the ground for vengeance, and this blood speaks better things. A believer whose conscience accuses him is being invited not to defend himself but to hear which blood is speaking.
roots_summary: Hebrew zaraq (H2236), to sprinkle or dash, and nazah (H5137), to sprinkle in drops; Greek rhantizō (G4472), to sprinkle — the priestly application of an accomplished sacrifice.
roots_lines: Hebrew nazah (H5137) — to spurt, sprinkle in drops; the finger-sprinkling of the mercy seat (Lev 16:14) and Isaiah's sprinkled nations (Isa 52:15).
Hebrew zaraq (H2236) — to scatter, sprinkle, dash; the blood dashed against the altar in the ordinary offerings.
Greek rhantismos (G4473) — sprinkling; “the blood of sprinkling” (Heb 12:24), and the sprinkled hearts of Heb 10:22.
usage: “Sprinkle it with his finger upon the mercy seat” — the sacrifice applied where God meets His people.
“Having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience” — the finger moved to the conscience.
“The blood of sprinkling, that speaketh better things than that of Abel” — two bloods, two messages.
